column3: A maternity ward where masked midwives hand you swaddled babies through a wall hatch — you never glimpse the delivery room. Creation happens behind the hatch.

column3: Pizza chain HQ mandates one ritual, makePizza() — but each franchise kitchen bakes its own pie: Chicago deep dish here, Napoli thin crust there.

column3: A Subway sandwich artist: bread? cheese? toasted? Each shout adds one layer, and only the final 'wrap it up!' (build) hands you the finished sub.

column6: Factory — a factory returns the object in one call; a builder accumulates many optional parts before build().

column3: Dolly the sheep on a photocopier: slam the lid on the prize ewe, press COPY, and an identical lamb trots warm out of the output tray.

column3: Highlander in a server room beheading every extra instance with a katana — 'There can be only one!' — then standing guard at the single door, getInstance().

column6: Static utility class — a singleton is a real instance (can implement interfaces, be passed around); statics cannot be substituted.

column3: The Highlander's katana rusts: one immortal hoarding all state, and every unit test must duel him at the locked door just to reset a flag.
column4: Singletons hide dependencies, create global mutable state, and weld tests to shared instances — prefer one instance wired via DI.
column5: Config.getInstance() buried deep vs constructor(config) — the second declares its needs
column6: 'One instance' vs 'global access' — a single instance is fine; the smell is the global access point that hides coupling.

column3: Bowling alley shoe counter: nobody buys shoes — you borrow a disinfectant-sprayed pair, bowl, return them, and the next bowler laces up the same pair.

column5: HikariCP database connection pool; ThreadPoolExecutor worker threads
column6: Flyweight — pooled objects are borrowed exclusively then returned; flyweights are immutable and shared by everyone at once.

column3: A vending machine bolted to the class wall: press the labeled button 'valueOf' and it may hand you a chilled cached can rather than brew a new one.
column4: A named static method that returns instances, enabling caching, subtype returns, and readable names that raw constructors cannot offer.
column5: Integer.valueOf(127) returns a cached instance; List.of(1,2,3); Optional.empty()
column6: GoF Factory Method — GoF's relies on subclass polymorphism to pick the product; static factories are just well-named static creators.

column3: A Murphy bed that stays hidden in the wall until the teenager's first yawn — then WHAM, it unfolds. Until that first yawn the room is empty and cheap.
column4: Defers costly object creation until the moment of first use, trading startup cost for a check (and locking care) on first access.
column5: if (instance == null) instance = new Heavy(); — double-checked locking when threaded
column6: Eager initialization — eager pays at load time and is trivially thread-safe; lazy pays on first access and needs synchronization.

column3: Scaffolding around a cathedral: nothing new is born on site — pipes, wraps, and bridges just join existing stones into a grander shape.
column4: GoF pattern family for composing classes and objects into larger flexible structures — mostly by wrapping or nesting existing pieces.
column5: Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy
column6: Creational patterns — structural arrange objects that already exist; creational decide how objects come into being.

column3: An EU wall plug jammed into a US socket via a chunky travel adapter cube — same electricity flowing, prongs reshaped. The cube speaks both pin languages.
column4: Wraps an object to convert its incompatible interface into the one clients expect, without changing either side.
column5: java.io.InputStreamReader adapts InputStream (bytes) to Reader (chars)
column6: Decorator — adapter CHANGES the interface; decorator keeps the same interface and adds behavior.

column3: A Christmas tree gaining lights, then tinsel, then baubles — at every layer it still answers to 'tree', just fancier each time you wrap it.
column4: Wraps an object behind the SAME interface to add responsibilities dynamically; wrappers stack in layers.
column5: new BufferedInputStream(new GZIPInputStream(new FileInputStream(f)))
column6: Proxy — decorator adds features and the client stacks it knowingly; proxy controls ACCESS and usually hides that it wraps. | cf. 328 Decorator (déjà pris): 328 is the language feature wrapping a FUNCTION; 612 the GoF pattern wrapping an OBJECT behind its own interface

column3: A hotel concierge desk: one calm smiling face; behind the wall, kitchens, laundries, and boilers roar. You just say 'dinner at eight'.
column4: Puts one simple front-door interface over a tangled subsystem so common tasks take one call instead of many.
column5: requests.get(url) hides sockets, TLS, redirects, pooling — Python requests library
column6: Adapter — facade SIMPLIFIES a whole subsystem; adapter CONVERTS one interface into another expected one.

column3: A celebrity's body double signs autographs at the studio gate; only vetted fans are ever walked back to the real star's trailer.
column4: A stand-in exposing the same interface as the real object while controlling access — lazy loading, caching, auth, or remoting.
column5: Hibernate lazy-loading entity proxies; RPC client stubs; nginx reverse proxy
column6: Decorator — proxy manages the real object's access and lifecycle on its own; decorator just layers on behavior the client composes.

column3: Russian nesting dolls that all answer paint(): tap the outermost doll and every doll nested inside paints itself too, down to the tiniest.
column4: Arranges objects into part-whole trees where leaves and containers share one interface, so clients treat both uniformly.
column5: Panel.draw() calls draw() on children — buttons and nested panels alike
column6: Decorator — decorator wraps exactly ONE child to extend it; composite holds MANY children to aggregate them.

column3: A drawbridge between two castle towers — the Shapes tower and the Renderers tower — each growing new floors independently while the bridge carries calls across.
column4: Splits an abstraction from its implementation into two independent hierarchies joined by composition, so both vary freely.
column5: Shape(renderer): Circle/Square x OpenGL/SVG = 2+2 classes, not 4 combined ones
column6: Adapter — adapter retrofits already-incompatible code; bridge is designed up front to prevent a class-combination explosion.

column3: A forest of a million trees pinned to ONE cardboard oak cut-out: each pin holds only an (x,y) tag; the heavy artwork exists exactly once.
column4: Shares immutable intrinsic state among many objects, keeping variable extrinsic state outside, so huge object counts stay cheap.
column5: Java String interning pool; one glyph object per character shared across a document
column6: Object pool — flyweights are immutable and shared simultaneously; pooled objects are mutable and borrowed exclusively.

column3: Four gift-wrappers at one mall kiosk: one reshapes the box, one adds ribbons, one guards it behind glass, one hides a messy pile under a single bow.
column4: Four wrappers, four intents: adapter converts the interface, decorator adds behavior, proxy controls access, facade simplifies many.
column5: All look like wrap(obj) in code — ask WHY it wraps to name the pattern
column6: All four are structurally identical wrapping — the discriminator is intent, never the code shape.

column3: Two translators: one was RAISED bilingual, both bloodlines inherited; the other carries a phrasebook in her handbag — composition she can swap.
column4: An adapter can inherit the adaptee (class adapter, needs multiple inheritance) or hold it by composition (object adapter, the usual way).
column5: class A extends Legacy implements Target vs class A implements Target { Legacy l; }
column6: Both are still Adapter — the split is inheritance vs composition of the adaptee, not a different pattern.

column3: A theater rehearsal with fixed actors but a director endlessly redrawing WHO cues WHOM — the patterns are his laminated cueing diagrams.
column4: GoF pattern family assigning responsibilities and communication between objects — who talks to whom, when, and how loosely.
column5: Observer, Strategy, Command, State, Memento, Iterator, Visitor, Mediator...
column6: Structural patterns — structural freeze object composition; behavioral choreograph runtime interaction and algorithm choice.

column3: A lighthouse blinks once and every ship's bell on the horizon rings itself — each ship had signed the lighthouse's ledger to be notified.
column4: A subject keeps a list of subscribers and notifies them automatically when its state changes — one-to-many, publisher pushes.
column5: button.addEventListener('click', fn); RxJS subject.subscribe(observer)
column6: Pub/sub — observers register directly WITH the subject; pub/sub inserts a broker so parties never know each other.

column3: A caddie's golf bag: same golfer, same swing, but you pull driver, wedge, or putter per hole — the bag hands you an algorithm shaped like a club.
column4: Encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind one interface so the client can pick or swap them at runtime.
column5: Collections.sort(list, comparator); compressor = new GzipStrategy()
column6: State — strategy is chosen by the CLIENT and strategies ignore each other; states switch THEMSELVES as the object transitions.

column3: A diner order spike: every shouted order becomes a paper ticket stabbed onto the spike — queueable, re-cookable, or torn up to undo.
column4: Reifies a request as an object carrying receiver plus parameters, enabling queues, logs, retries, and undo.
column5: editor.execute(new PasteCommand(clipboard)); Celery task queues
column6: Strategy — command packages ONE invocation (verb plus args) to defer or undo; strategy packages an algorithm choice with no undo semantics.

column3: A vending machine possessed by moods: the CoinInserted spirit grabs the wheel, then hands it to Dispensing. Same chassis, a new driver at every stage.
column4: An object delegates behavior to a current-state object and swaps it on transitions, replacing sprawling conditionals.
column5: TCPConnection delegates open()/close() to Closed, Listening, Established objects
column6: Strategy — identical UML, but states know their siblings and trigger their own transitions; strategies are independent and client-picked.

column3: A wax-sealed envelope of your diary page: the archivist stores it but can never read it; only YOU may crack the seal and become Tuesday-you again.
column4: Captures an object's private state in an opaque token so it can be restored later without breaking encapsulation.
column5: m = editor.save(); ...; editor.restore(m) — game save slots work this way
column6: Command undo — command replays inverse operations; memento snapshots and reinstates whole state blobs.

column3: A cardboard-cutout security guard propped by the door: patrol() does nothing at all, but nobody ever trips over an empty guard post.
column4: A do-nothing implementation of an interface used in place of null, removing repetitive null checks from clients.
column5: class NullLogger { log(msg) {} }; return Collections.emptyList() not null
column6: Optional/Maybe — Optional forces callers to CHECK for presence; a null object silently absorbs calls with safe defaults.

column3: Pancakes stack up as you type; Ctrl+Z peels the top pancake and un-fries it back into batter, while the redo plate waits to re-fry it.
column4: Executed commands are pushed onto a stack; undo pops and reverses them (or restores mementos), redo replays from a second stack.
column5: undoStack.push(cmd); undo(): c = undoStack.pop(); c.unexecute(); redoStack.push(c)
column6: Event sourcing — undo stacks are session-local UI history; event sourcing is the persisted system of record.

column3: The lighthouse keeps ringing doorbells of houses whose owners moved out years ago — the copper wires (references) alone hold the empty houses up.
column4: Observers that never unsubscribe stay strongly referenced by the subject, causing memory leaks and ghost notifications.
column5: Fix: removeEventListener on teardown; or WeakReference listener lists
column6: Generic memory leak — here the SUBJECT holds the reference, so 'unused' observers are uncollectable and still receive events.

column3: The golf caddie is fired and replaced by a single floating glove: no bag, no clubs, you just hand over the bare hand — the function itself.
column4: In languages with first-class functions, a bare lambda replaces the one-method strategy class — same pattern, no ceremony.
column5: sorted(xs, key=lambda x: x.age) instead of writing an AgeComparator class
column6: 'The pattern disappeared' — the intent (pluggable algorithm) remains; only the class boilerplate evaporated.

column3: A museum audio-guide wand: press NEXT and it leads you room by room in order — you never see the curator's storage maps or basement shelving.
column4: Provides sequential access to a collection's elements through a standard cursor interface without exposing internal structure.
column5: for x in xs uses __iter__/__next__; Java it.hasNext()/it.next()
column6: Iterable — the iterable is the collection that VENDS iterators; the iterator is the one-use cursor itself.

column3: A Mad Libs card: the plot is printed in permanent ink; subclasses may only scribble words into the blanks, then the card reads itself aloud.
column4: A base-class method fixes an algorithm's skeleton and defers specific steps to subclass hook overrides.
column5: JUnit setUp()/test/tearDown(); HttpServlet.service() dispatching to your doGet()
column6: Strategy — template method varies steps via INHERITANCE, fixed at compile time; strategy swaps whole algorithms via composition at runtime.

column3: A tax inspector walking a village: each house opens its OWN door (accept), and the inspector whips out exactly the right form for that house type.
column4: Moves an operation out of a stable object structure into a visitor object; elements call accept(v) which calls back v.visitX(this).
column5: ast.accept(prettyPrinter); compiler passes: TypeCheckVisitor, CodeGenVisitor
column6: Iterator — iterator merely walks the elements; visitor dispatches type-specific operations via double dispatch.

column3: An air-traffic control tower: planes never radio each other directly — every 'may I land?' routes through the tower, or metal rains from the sky.
column4: Centralizes many-to-many communication: colleagues talk only to a mediator hub, which coordinates who reacts and how.
column5: ChatRoom.send(msg, from) routes to members; dialog controller coordinating widgets
column6: Observer — observer broadcasts one-to-many blindly; mediator encodes explicit pairwise coordination LOGIC inside the hub.

column3: An office complaint slip climbing desks: the intern shrugs and passes it up, the manager shrugs — the slip crawls upward until someone finally stamps it.
column4: Passes a request along a linked chain of handlers; each one either handles it or forwards it to the next.
column5: Express middleware fn(req, res, next); Java servlet filter chains
column6: Decorator — same wrapping shape, but decorators ALL run to add behavior; chain handlers may short-circuit and one 'owns' the request.

column3: A tiny UN inside your program: one translator booth per grammar rule; a sentence passes booth to booth down the parse tree until meaning drips out the bottom.
column4: Represents each grammar rule as a class and evaluates sentences by walking the resulting syntax tree.
column5: regex engines; SQL WHERE-clause evaluators; expr.interpret(context)
column6: Visitor on an AST — interpreter puts eval() IN the node classes; visitor extracts operations out of them.

column3: A sommelier sliding one glass down the bar through a chain of stations that each add a note - the same glass keeps traveling, collecting flavor, until someone finally drinks it (executes).
column4: Methods return the receiver (or builder) so calls chain into a readable sentence that executes at the end.
column5: QueryBuilder().select('id').where('age > 21').limit(10).run()
column6: vs builder pattern (603): builder is about assembling a complex product; fluent chaining is the SYNTAX builders often wear

column3: A casting agent snatches your headshot at the door: 'We'll call YOU.' Months later the phone rings with your one scene — the hook method.
column4: 'Don't call us, we'll call you': frameworks and template skeletons invoke your code at the right moment; you never drive their control flow.
column5: React calls your render(); Spring calls your @Bean methods; you never call the framework's main loop
column6: Dependency inversion principle — DIP concerns which ABSTRACTION you depend on; Hollywood concerns who holds control FLOW.

column3: Museum two ways: grip the audio-wand and press NEXT yourself, or slump into the tram that drives past every exhibit while you just hand it your eyes (callback).
column4: External iterators let the client pull items with next(); internal iterators take a callback and the collection drives the loop.
column5: it.next() (external) vs xs.forEach(f) / xs.map(f) (internal)
column6: Push vs pull streams — same duality: external is pull (client paces), internal is push (producer paces).

column3: A knight in five stacked suits of armor clanking off to fetch tea — AbstractTeaFactoryVisitorProxy — who can no longer bend his arm enough to pour.
column4: Applying patterns speculatively adds indirection without need; reach for one only when its specific force is actually present.
column5: One if/else beats a Strategy hierarchy for two stable cases
column6: YAGNI — YAGNI rejects unneeded FEATURES; patternitis is unneeded STRUCTURE around features you do need.

column3: A wedding cake you may only eat top-down: each tier rests squarely on the tier beneath and never, ever licks upward.
column4: Organizes code into horizontal layers (UI, application, domain, data) where each layer depends only on those below it.
column5: Controller -> Service -> Repository -> Database
column6: Hexagonal — layered stacks dependencies downward toward the DB; hexagonal points everything inward toward the domain.

column3: A queen bee in the center cell of a honeycomb: each of the six waxed walls has a socket, and worker bees plug tools in from outside — the queen never leaves.
column4: Puts the domain core at the center behind ports; adapters at the edges translate between the core and every external technology.
column5: Core defines OrderRepository port; PostgresOrderRepository adapter plugs in from outside
column6: Layered — hexagonal is symmetric (DB and UI are both mere adapters); layered treats the database as the special bottom.

column3: USB sockets molded into the honeycomb's wax walls: the hive dictates each socket's shape, and any gadget arriving from outside must match the hole.
column4: A technology-neutral interface owned by the core that declares what the application needs or offers — the socket, not the plug.
column5: interface PaymentGateway { charge(amount) } — declared inside the domain module
column6: Adapter — the port is the interface defined inside the core; the adapter is the implementation living outside it.

column3: Left wall of the honeycomb: woodpeckers hammering requests IN. Right wall: the hive's own tubes squirting honey OUT into jars. Same walls, opposite arrows.
column4: Driving (primary) adapters call INTO the core — HTTP controllers, CLIs; driven (secondary) adapters are called BY the core — DB, mail.
column5: REST controller -> core (driving); core -> SmtpMailer (driven)
column6: GoF Adapter — here 'adapter' means any tech-specific edge component, not interface conversion per se.

column3: An onion whose core never cries: knives, tears, and supermarket stickers stay on the outer skins; the center ring has never even smelled a fridge (framework).
column4: Concentric rings — entities, use cases, interface adapters, frameworks — with all source dependencies pointing inward toward the domain.
column5: UseCase imports Entity; Controller imports UseCase; never the reverse
column6: Hexagonal — same spirit; clean/onion prescribe named rings, hexagonal just says core-plus-ports. All obey 'point inward'.

column3: A one-way pilgrimage road spiraling into a mountain shrine: carts roll inward only, and the monks inside have never once heard the market's name.
column4: Source-code dependencies may only point inward: inner circles know nothing — not even names — of anything in outer circles.
column5: Domain never imports Spring, HTTP, or SQL; outer code implements domain-owned interfaces
column6: Dependency inversion principle — DIP is the class-level technique; the dependency rule is the architecture-wide policy it enforces.

column3: A decontamination airlock between your gleaming lab and a rusty factory: every crate gets unpacked, scrubbed, and repacked into YOUR containers before entering.
column4: A translating boundary that converts a legacy or external model into your own, so foreign concepts never leak into your domain.
column5: LegacyCrmClient -> AclTranslator -> Customer (your model, your terms)
column6: Plain adapter — an ACL translates whole MODELS and semantics between contexts, not just one interface's method signatures.

column3: A monk copying scripture with a feather quill while gadget salesmen pound on the monastery door — the manuscripts calmly outlive every gadget fad.
column4: Keep entities and business rules in plain objects with zero framework imports, so the core outlives and ignores infrastructure churn.
column5: Domain layer: no @Entity, no HttpRequest — pure classes and functions only
column6: 'No frameworks anywhere' — frameworks are fine in OUTER rings; the rule bans them only from the domain core.

column3: Two office towers: in one, the elevator only ever descends a single floor per ride (strict); in the other you may plunge straight from penthouse to basement archives.
column4: Strict layering lets a layer call only the layer directly beneath it; relaxed layering permits skipping layers downward for pragmatism.
column5: Controller calling Repository directly = relaxed layering (skips Service)
column6: Layer violation — skipping DOWNWARD can be sanctioned policy; any upward dependency is always a violation.

column3: Wedding cake vs wedding venues: one cake's sponge tiers (layers) can all sit on a single table, or be couriered to three different cities (tiers).
column4: Layers are logical separations within a codebase; tiers are physical deployment units — a 3-layer app can run on a single tier.
column5: Django app (3 layers) on one server = 1 tier; move DB to its own host = 2 tiers
column6: N-tier marketing speak — count machines for tiers, count module boundaries for layers.

column3: Castle walls with one guarded gate: merchants trade only at the gate's counter, and whatever chaos brews inside the walls never crosses the moat.
column4: A module hides its internals behind a small public interface; the boundary is where the contract lives and change stops propagating.
column5: Java module exports; TypeScript index.ts re-exporting only the public API
column6: Namespace/folder — a folder merely groups files; a boundary additionally enforces WHAT is visible and hides the rest.

column3: A trapeze artist wearing ropes: ropes others pull taut on her (Ca) hold her steady; ropes SHE grips outward (Ce) make her sway. Sway fraction = instability.
column4: Dependency counts quantify coupling: afferent Ca (who needs me), efferent Ce (whom I need), instability I = Ce/(Ca+Ce).
column5: I near 0 = stable core lib; I near 1 = top-level app; JDepend/ArchUnit report these
column6: Cohesion — coupling measures dependence BETWEEN modules; cohesion measures belonging-together WITHIN one.

column3: A hardware store reorganized by project instead of material: the build-a-birdhouse aisle holds its own nails, wood and paint, so one job touches one aisle.
column4: Group code by business capability, not technical layer: feature packages localize change; layer packages scatter every feature across the whole tree.
column5: orders/ (model+api+db together) vs models/, views/, controllers/ each holding a slice of orders
column6: vs layered architecture (64x): layers can still exist INSIDE a feature package; the question is the top-level folder axis

column3: A robotic LEGO butler reads your blueprint at dawn and snaps the entire castle together before you wake — you never touch a single brick yourself.
column4: A framework that reads wiring configuration, builds the whole object graph, and injects dependencies automatically, managing lifetimes.
column5: Spring ApplicationContext; .NET IServiceCollection; Guice Injector
column6: DI the pattern — DI needs no container; 'pure DI' wires by hand in main(). The container merely automates the wiring.

column3: A spaceship that physically cannot launch until every crew member is strapped in at ignition — and the hatch welds itself shut after liftoff (immutability).
column4: Dependencies arrive as constructor parameters, making them mandatory, visible, and enabling immutable, always-valid objects.
column5: constructor(private repo: Repo) {} — compile error if a caller omits it
column6: Setter/field injection — those allow half-initialized objects and hidden requirements; constructor injection fails fast at build time.

column3: Three mountaineers roped in a closed circle: when one slips, all three dangle together — and no single climber can ever be rescued (released) alone.
column4: Mutual dependencies among packages weld them into one un-reusable, un-releasable lump; keep the dependency graph acyclic (ADP).
column5: A->B->C->A: touching C rebuilds all; fix by extracting an interface package
column6: Class-level circular imports — same disease at file scale; ADP concerns released package/module units.

column3: A pegboard power-tool wall: the bare drill body (core) accepts any snap-on head — sander, whisk, saw — sold years later by total strangers.
column4: A minimal core defines extension-point interfaces and discovers plugins at runtime, so features ship and load independently.
column5: VS Code extensions; ESLint plugins; Java ServiceLoader discovery
column6: Library use — the app calls a library; a plugin is called BY the core through the core's own interface (control inverted).

column3: Employees sneak to a dusty basement vending machine for their tools: the org chart (constructor) lists no tools at all — until tests find the machine empty and everything jams.
column4: Components fetch dependencies from a global registry — an anti-pattern versus DI because it hides real dependencies and hurts testing.
column5: ServiceLocator.get('mailer') deep inside a method — invisible in any signature
column6: DI container — the container injects from OUTSIDE at composition time; a locator is called from INSIDE, coupling code to the registry.

column3: One grand florist stand at the app's front door where every bouquet (object graph) is arranged before opening hour — no flowers are ever cut in back offices.
column4: The single place near the entry point where the whole object graph is composed; nothing else news up long-lived collaborators.
column5: main() { app = new App(new PgRepo(cfg), new SmtpMailer(cfg)); app.run(); }
column6: Scattered new()s — the smell it cures; construction knowledge lives in ONE root, not sprinkled through business code.

column3: Hammocks tied to old oaks, never to saplings: swinging sleepers (changing apps) hang off thick trunks (stable cores). Tie an oak to a sapling and both crash down.
column4: Depend in the direction of stability: volatile packages may depend on stable ones, never the reverse.
column5: app (I~0.9) -> utils (I~0.1) fine; core depending on an experimental lib = violation
column6: Stable-abstractions principle — SAP adds that stable packages should also be ABSTRACT; SDP only orders the arrows.

column3: A puppet theater: the puppet (view) dances on stage, the puppeteer's hands (controller) translate the audience's shouts, the script binder backstage (model) holds the story.
column4: Splits UI into Model (state and logic), View (presentation), Controller (input handling); views render from the model.
column5: Rails: route -> UsersController -> User model -> ERB view
column6: MVP — in MVC the view may read the model directly; in MVP a presenter mediates everything and the view stays passive.

column3: A ventriloquist (presenter) with a wooden dummy (view): the dummy holds no thoughts of its own, moving its jaw exactly as the hand inside commands.
column4: A presenter takes all input, drives a passive view through an interface, and talks to the model — view and model never meet.
column5: Android pre-ViewModel: LoginPresenter calls LoginView.showError()
column6: MVVM — MVP's presenter calls view methods explicitly; MVVM's viewmodel exposes state and lets data binding do the syncing.

column3: A mirror-dance studio: the dancer (viewmodel) moves and the mirror (view) matches instantly — neither ever touches the other; the glass (binding) does all the work.
column4: A viewmodel exposes bindable state and commands; a data-binding layer keeps view and viewmodel in sync with no direct references.
column5: WPF, Knockout, Vue: <input v-model='name'> bound to a viewmodel field
column6: MVP — MVVM replaces the presenter's explicit view calls with declarative bindings; the viewmodel never knows the view exists.

column3: Two buckets on a pulley rope through a window: pour water into either bucket and the rope instantly levels them — sometimes sloshing back and forth mysteriously at 3am.
column4: Framework machinery auto-syncs view widgets and model fields in both directions, at the cost of harder-to-trace update flows.
column5: Angular [(ngModel)]='user.name' — edits flow field<->input automatically
column6: One-way binding — one-way re-renders the view FROM state only; edits return via explicit events, keeping the flow traceable.

column3: LEGO minifigs each carrying a tiny brain and wardrobe inside: snap a plaza together from figures, then snap one figure into a different set — it still works.
column4: UI built from self-contained components owning their markup, logic, and state, composed into trees like functions.
column5: React: <App><Header><SearchBar/></Header></App>
column6: Template partials — partials share markup only; components also encapsulate behavior and local state.

column3: A one-way water park: state pours down the slide into the views below; riders send wishes back up only via the message-balloon chimney (actions). No swimming upstream.
column4: State flows down as props and changes flow up as events or actions through one loop, making every mutation traceable.
column5: React: props down, onChange callbacks up; the Elm architecture loop
column6: Two-way binding — the very thing it replaces; syncing both ways is convenient but obscures who changed what.

column3: A courtroom for every click: the action files a case (dispatch), the judge-reducer reads old law plus case and pens ONE new law book — the whole town re-reads it.
column4: All state lives in one store; views dispatch actions, pure reducers compute the next state, and views re-render from it.
column5: dispatch({type:'ADD_TODO', text}); reducer: (state, action) => newState
column6: MVC — many controllers mutate models in place; Redux has one store and immutable transitions through pure functions.

column3: Two kids fight over one toy, so mom places it on the top shelf: now both must ask her (the common ancestor), and everyone sees the same toy.
column4: When siblings must share state, move it to their closest common ancestor and pass it down, keeping one source of truth.
column5: React: temperature state moved from two inputs into the parent Calculator
column6: Global store — lifting goes only as high as NEEDED; jumping straight to a global store couples everything to it.

column3: A restaurant split in two: the kitchen (container) sources and cooks everything; the plating artist (presentational) only arranges whatever lands on the plate.
column4: Container components fetch data and hold logic; presentational components just render props — data and looks kept separate.
column5: UserListContainer fetches, then renders <UserList users={users}/>
column6: Custom hooks — hooks now often replace containers by extracting logic without an extra component layer.

column3: A shy stagehand whose only job is pulling the curtain rope: he makes zero decisions, so nobody ever needs to audition (test) him — the whole play lives elsewhere.
column4: Split hard-to-test boundary code into a thin humble shell and a testable core, pushing all logic out of the untestable part.
column5: View just prints viewmodel fields; all formatting logic unit-tested in the viewmodel
column6: Facade — a facade simplifies a subsystem for callers; a humble object exists to move logic OUT of an untestable edge.

column3: A town-square bell: the baker rings 'bread's ready!' and walks away; whoever cares comes running. The baker knows no names and waits for no one.
column4: Components communicate by producing and reacting to events rather than calling each other, decoupling senders from receivers in time and knowledge.
column5: OrderPlaced event -> email service, inventory, analytics each react independently
column6: Request/response — a request needs the receiver up NOW and awaits an answer; an event is fire-and-forget to unknown listeners.

column3: Magazine subscriptions: writers mail issues to the 'Gardening' PO box; the postman fans copies out to the subscriber list. Authors never see a single address.
column4: Producers publish to named topics on a broker; subscribers receive by topic — neither side ever knows the other exists.
column5: Kafka topic 'orders'; Redis PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE; Google Pub/Sub
column6: Observer — observers register directly with the subject object; pub/sub interposes a broker and topic names between the parties.

column3: A doorbell rings with a note: 'package #42 arrived.' You still have to trudge to the depot and ask what's inside box 42.
column4: Thin events announce that something happened plus an ID; consumers call back to the source for details — small events, but coupled reads.
column5: {event:'OrderPlaced', orderId:42} -> consumer GETs /orders/42 for details
column6: Event-carried state transfer — fat events carry the data along, so no callback query is ever needed.

column3: The drone drops the WHOLE parcel on your porch, not a claim ticket: your own pantry (local copy) fills up, and you never visit the depot again.
column4: Events carry the full relevant state so consumers keep local copies and never query the source — availability up, duplication and staleness accepted.
column5: {event:'OrderPlaced', order:{id, items, total, address}} consumed into a local table
column6: Event notification — notification sends a pointer (go ask); ECST sends the payload (never ask).

column3: An accountant's ink ledger: nobody erases, ever; a mistake gets a correcting line, and today's balance is re-summed from page one whenever anyone asks.
column4: Persist every state change as an immutable event; current state is derived by replaying the log, which is the system of record.
column5: Account balance = fold(Deposited, Withdrawn...); snapshots speed up replay
column6: Audit log — an audit log is a side record; in event sourcing the log IS the primary data and state is just a projection.

column3: A restaurant with two doors: orders enter through the strict kitchen door (commands, checks), while diners browse the big glass buffet window (reads), pre-plated for speed.
column4: Splits the write model (commands, invariants) from read models (queries, projections) so each side scales and shapes data independently.
column5: POST -> domain aggregate; GET -> denormalized view table updated from events
column6: Event sourcing — often paired but independent; CQRS is two models, ES is log-as-truth. You can do CQRS over a plain SQL DB.

column3: A trip booked in dominoes: flight, hotel, car click down in turn; when the car rental topples, gnomes sprint back up the line standing hotel and flight dominoes upright again (compensations).
column4: A long-running distributed transaction as a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action to undo on failure.
column5: ReserveFlight -> ReserveHotel fails -> run CancelFlight compensation
column6: Two-phase commit — 2PC locks all parties for atomicity; sagas accept intermediate states and undo with business-level compensations.

column3: A stamp collector gluing envelopes by serial number into an album: the same envelope delivered twice gets a shrug — 'already glued in' — and hits the bin.
column4: Handlers detect and ignore duplicate deliveries — via message IDs or naturally idempotent writes — since brokers promise at-least-once.
column5: if processed_ids.contains(msg.id): skip; or UPSERT instead of INSERT
column6: Exactly-once delivery — a myth end-to-end; reality is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing to simulate it.

column3: Village gossip: grandma hears the wedding news a full day after the baker does, but by Sunday mass every single villager tells the identical story.
column4: Replicas may briefly disagree after a write; absent new updates all converge to the same state — reads can be stale meanwhile.
column5: DNS propagation; DynamoDB default reads; read-your-writes sessions as a remedy
column6: Strong consistency — strong makes every read see the latest write, paying latency and availability (CAP) for the privilege.

column3: The love letter is sealed into the same envelope as the rent check: one lick, one stamp — both arrive or neither does. The mailroom clerk (relay) does the actual posting.
column4: Write events to an outbox table in the SAME DB transaction as the state change; a relay publishes them later — no lost or phantom events.
column5: INSERT order; INSERT outbox(event); COMMIT; Debezium/poller ships rows to Kafka
column6: Dual write — the bug it fixes: writing DB then broker separately can succeed on one and silently fail on the other.

column3: One granite boulder versus a mosaic of pebbles joined by strings: the boulder moves whole or not at all; pebbles travel alone, but the strings (network) fray and tangle.
column4: One deployable with in-process calls versus many independently deployable services with network calls — simplicity traded for autonomy plus ops cost.
column5: One Rails app on one box vs Netflix's hundreds of services
column6: Modular monolith — modules give boundaries WITHOUT the network; distribution is about deployment, not code structure.

column3: Cutting a birthday cake along the frosting roses, never through them: slice through a rose (capability) and both plates need each other's crumbs forever after.
column4: Draw service lines around business capabilities that change together, so one team can deploy without synchronizing with others.
column5: Billing, Shipping, Catalog services — not 'the controllers service'
column6: Bounded context — a great default source of boundaries; a service boundary adds deployment, team, and runtime autonomy on top.

column3: A highway keeps the rusty old bridge open while the new one rises alongside: signs read '/v1 left lane, /v2 right' — and nobody's car falls into the river.
column4: Publish breaking changes under a new explicit version while old versions keep serving, so clients migrate on their own schedule.
column5: GET /v2/users; Stripe-Version header; media-type versioning in Accept
column6: Backward-compatible change — additive changes (a new optional field) need NO new version; version only for breaks.

column3: Grandma's recipe card with extra sticky notes stapled on: old cooks simply ignore the staples and the cake still rises — but no one may ever cross out a line.
column4: Evolve APIs additively — add optional fields, never rename, remove, or retype — while clients ignore unknown fields (tolerant reader).
column5: Protobuf: never reuse field numbers; JSON consumers skip unknown keys
column6: Forward compatibility — backward: new server keeps old clients working; forward: old code tolerates NEW data it doesn't know.

column3: Architects sign blueprints before one brick is laid: plumber and electrician build in parallel to the same drawing, and the inspector (contract test) checks walls against paper.
column4: Write and agree the API contract (OpenAPI, protobuf, AsyncAPI) before implementing; both sides generate code and test against it.
column5: openapi.yaml -> generate server stubs + client SDK; Pact contract tests in CI
column6: Code-first with generated docs — docs derived from code drift with it; contract-first makes the spec the source of truth.

column3: Personal shoppers per customer: the mobile shopper packs a tiny pre-chewed lunchbox, the web shopper loads a full banquet cart — both raid the same warehouses.
column4: A dedicated backend per client type (web, mobile, TV) that aggregates and reshapes downstream APIs to that UI's exact needs.
column5: Netflix: separate API edge services for iOS vs TV clients
column6: API gateway — a gateway is one generic front door (auth, routing); a BFF is client-specific and owned by that client's team.

column3: A strangler fig vine wrapping a great old oak: root by root it steals the light, and years later the vine IS the tree — hollow bark where the oak once stood.
column4: Incrementally replace a legacy system by routing slices of traffic to new services growing around it, until the old core can be deleted.
column5: Proxy routes /invoices to the new service, everything else to legacy; migrate route by route
column6: Big-bang rewrite — the fig migrates in shippable slices with rollback; a rewrite bets everything on one cut-over day.

column3: Chain-gang prisoners in separate cells: officially independent, yet shackled ankle-to-ankle straight through the walls — one man shifting drags every cell block.
column4: Services that must be deployed, versioned, or changed together — network overhead plus tight coupling; the worst of both worlds.
column5: Smells: shared database across services, lockstep releases, sync call chains 5 deep
column6: Honest monolith — a monolith is coupling in-process, cheaply; the smell is PAYING distribution costs without gaining autonomy.

column3: A castle gatehouse: one drawbridge where guards check papers, count entrants, and point carts to the right courtyard — the inner keeps have no doors to the outside world.
column4: A single entry point in front of services handling cross-cutting edge concerns — routing, auth, rate limiting, TLS — so each service doesn't.
column5: Kong/Envoy/AWS API Gateway: /users -> user-svc after JWT check and rate limit
column6: BFF — a gateway is one shared generic edge; a BFF is per-client and reshapes payloads for that specific UI.

column3: An apartment building with individually locked units and one street address: tenants (modules) cannot wander into each other's kitchens, yet there is exactly one front door to maintain.
column4: One deployable whose internal modules keep strict boundaries and own their data — microservice discipline without the network.
column5: Shopify's Rails core with packwerk-enforced component boundaries
column6: Big ball of mud — the difference is ENFORCED module boundaries; mud has one deployable AND no interior walls.

column3: A ship's crew who call every rope by its exact name: shout 'halyard!' and all hands grab the same line. Mutter 'that ropey thing' and the mast comes down.
column4: One precise shared vocabulary, spoken by developers and domain experts alike, used identically in conversation, models, and code.
column5: Experts say 'the policy lapses' -> class Policy { lapse() } — never 'deactivate'
column6: Company jargon — jargon drifts per department; ubiquitous language is deliberately unified WITHIN one bounded context.

column3: A man with a barcode tattooed on his ankle: he ages, dyes his hair, changes his name twice — the scanner still beeps the same ID. He IS his barcode.
column4: A domain object defined by a stable identity that persists through time, not by its attributes, which may all change.
column5: Customer #881 changes address and email — still the same Customer
column6: Value object — swap every field of an entity and it is still 'it'; a value object with different fields IS a different value.

column3: Two identical 2x4 red LEGO bricks: shuffle them behind your back and nobody can ever tell. To 'change' one's color you don't repaint — you pick up a different brick.
column4: An immutable object defined entirely by its attribute values, with no identity; equal fields mean interchangeable objects.
column5: Money(10,'EUR') == Money(10,'EUR'); LocalDate; Coordinates(lat, lng)
column6: Entity — entities compare by ID and may mutate; value objects compare by all fields and should be immutable.

column3: A grape bunch held only by its stem: to move, sell, or inspect any grape you must lift the stem (root). Pluck a grape directly and invariant juice spills everywhere.
column4: A cluster of entities and values with one root as sole entry point; the root enforces invariants and is saved as one transactional unit.
column5: Order (root) owns OrderLines; order.addLine() enforces the total; repo saves the Order whole
column6: Plain object graph — an aggregate forbids outside references to its internals; only the root's ID crosses the boundary.

column3: A magic library counter: whisper 'Order 42' and the librarian slides you the whole bound volume; hand one back and it is filed. You never see the stacks (SQL).
column4: A collection-like abstraction for retrieving and persisting whole aggregates, keeping domain code free of query and storage detail.
column5: orders.findById(id); orders.save(order) — interface in domain, impl in infrastructure
column6: DAO — a DAO mirrors tables and rows; a repository speaks in whole aggregates and domain terms, one per aggregate root.

column3: Two embassies on one street: inside each fence 'visa' means something precise — and different. Cross a gate and your papers must be re-translated.
column4: An explicit boundary inside which one model and language hold consistently; the same word may map to a different model next door.
column5: 'Product' in Catalog (photos, copy) vs in Shipping (weight, dimensions)
column6: Microservice — contexts are model and language boundaries; a service is a deployment unit. Often 1:1, but not necessarily.

column3: A war-room map with strings between embassy pins, each string labeled 'who obeys whom': some pairs share a treaty (shared kernel), others hide behind translators (ACL).
column4: Documenting relationships between bounded contexts — partnership, customer/supplier, conformist, ACL, shared kernel — and who adapts to whom.
column5: Sales conforms to the legacy ERP's model; Payments shields itself via an ACL
column6: Architecture diagram — boxes-and-arrows show calls; a context map shows POWER and model-translation relationships.

column3: A town crier's scroll nailed to the market post: 'OrderShipped, this third of June!' — past tense, sealed in wax; anyone may read and react, no one may edit.
column4: An immutable record, named in past tense in the ubiquitous language, of something meaningful that happened in the domain.
column5: class OrderShipped { orderId, occurredAt }; published after the commit
column6: Command — a command asks for something TO happen (imperative, refusable); an event states it already DID (immutable fact).

column3: A freelance notary who owns no house: he walks between households (aggregates) to officiate exchanges no single family could sign alone, then leaves carrying nothing.
column4: A stateless domain operation that spans multiple aggregates or fits no single entity, expressed in the ubiquitous language.
column5: TransferService.transfer(fromAccount, toAccount, amount) — touches two aggregates
column6: Application service — app services orchestrate use cases (transactions, auth, DTOs); domain services hold BUSINESS rules spanning entities.

column3: A gym full of mannequins in workout clothes: perfectly shaped bodies (data) that cannot lift a single dumbbell; trainers (services) drag their limbs around for them.
column4: A smell where entities are bags of getters and setters and all behavior lives in service classes — OO shape without OO benefits.
column5: OrderService.calcTotal(order) vs order.total() — logic exiled from its data
column6: DTO — DTOs are SUPPOSED to be dumb carriers at boundaries; the smell is DOMAIN objects being that dumb.
